title: When to Walk Away from a Project
summary: Every project has a hard middle, and some are real dead ends. How to tell them apart, try one honest fix, set kill criteria with a date, and leave well if you go.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

faqs.q: How do I know if I should leave a project?
faqs.a: Watch how the project responds to new information. If decisions stick, risks get handled and feedback changes the plan, you're probably in a hard middle worth sticking with. If for months the same questions keep coming back, decisions keep getting reopened and ownership comes without authority, it may be a dead end.

Annie Duke's term for conditions, set in advance, that tell you when to stop. The useful ones pair a state with a date, for example: if we still have no owner who can decide scope by the end of next month, I'll ask to move teams.

faqs.q: How do I leave a project without burning bridges?
faqs.a: Tell your manager first, write a handoff with the current state, open decisions and known risks, and describe problems without blaming individuals. Most stuck projects are full of people doing their best inside a structure that isn't working.

html:
It's Thursday evening and the project board looks the same as it did a month ago. A few cards changed columns. A few new risks got added. One decision has been renamed three times without getting any clearer. You close the laptop, and the tiredness isn't really from the work. It's from the feeling that effort has stopped turning into progress.

Walking away from a project sounds a lot like giving up, and sometimes it is. Every project worth doing has a hard middle: the early excitement is gone, the problems are plain to see and the finish line isn't in sight yet. Leaving at that point usually just trades a hard problem for a comfortable one. Other projects are different. Staying slowly costs you your judgment, your health and sometimes your integrity. This post covers how to tell the two apart, how to try fixing things before you go, and how to leave well if you do.

Hard middle or dead end?

From the inside, both feel like being stuck. The difference shows up in how the project responds to new information. A rough guide:

Hard middleDead end
GoalDifficult, but people can explain itChanges often, and nobody names the trade-off
DecisionsSomeone makes them and they stickKeep getting reopened, or nobody owns them
RisksRaised and dealt with, even if slowlyRaised, nodded at, then left alone
FeedbackChanges the planChanges the slides
QualityTime for it is tight but realRequested, while the time for it keeps getting cut
OwnershipComes with the authority to actComes without any authority
MoodTired, but still learningTired, and the same questions keep coming back

No single row decides it. But if most of your answers land in the right-hand column and have stayed there for months, persistence may have stopped being discipline. It might just be stubbornness with a good work ethic.

Why we stay too long

Part of it is plain psychology. In 1985, Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer described the sunk cost effect as "a greater tendency to continue an endeavor once an investment in money, effort, or time has been made" (The Psychology of Sunk Cost). In one of their studies, theater-goers who'd paid full price for season tickets went to more plays in the first half of the season than people who'd been given a discount. Same plays, same season. The only difference was what they'd already paid.

Projects work the same way, except the currency is months of your life and the promises you've made to your team. Annie Duke, a former professional poker player who now writes about decision making, puts it neatly: we think of waste as a backward-looking problem, when it's really a forward-looking one (in conversation with David Epstein). The months you've spent are gone whatever you decide. The real question is what the next three months will buy.

Try to fix it first

Before you leave, give the project one honest chance to change. A vague complaint is easy to dismiss. A clear trade-off is much harder to ignore.

  • Write the problem down in two or three sentences. "We've reopened the pricing decision three times since June, so nobody can plan past the next sprint."
  • Ask for the specific decision you need, and name who can make it.
  • Offer a smaller scope that could actually ship.
  • Put the risk in terms the business can weigh: time, money, customer trust, compliance, team capacity.

Then ask yourself what would have to change for you to stay. Not everything, just enough. A real owner. Scope frozen for two weeks. Time to fix the flaky test suite. Permission to cut one risky feature. A clear answer on whether the date or the quality bar wins. If you can't name a reasonable condition, you may already know your answer. If you name one and nobody responds, that's information too.

Duke calls these conditions "kill criteria", and she says they need a date as well as a state: "You need to put a deadline on it." She also suggests setting them the moment you first catch yourself thinking "maybe I should quit." For a project, that might be: "If we still don't have an owner who can decide scope by the end of next month, I'll ask to move teams." Write it down early, before the feelings pile up, and the later decision depends much less on what kind of week you're having.

Two lines worth taking seriously

The first is your values. Some projects ask for compromises that are merely uncomfortable. Others ask for compromises that make you smaller. Shipping a feature with known accessibility gaps and a plan to fix them is one thing. Hiding a security risk from users is another. Living through a messy migration is one thing. Being asked to mislead a customer is another. You can bend on the first kind. The second kind is where leaving protects the engineer you're trying to become.

The second is your health, and it doesn't have to be dramatic to count. The WHO describes burn-out as a syndrome "resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed," with three signs: exhaustion, growing mental distance or cynicism about your job, and reduced professional efficacy (WHO, 2019). A project that eats your evenings, interrupts your weekends and still won't make clearer decisions is borrowing from people without writing down the debt. At that point, ask whether the project has earned what it's costing you. Whether you're tough enough to keep going is the less useful question.

If you go, leave well

How you leave still matters, both to the people who stay and to your own standards.

  • Write down what you know: the current state, open decisions, the risks you see and the corners of the code only you understand.
  • Hand over risks plainly. No told-you-so, no settling scores.
  • Don't retell the story so you're the only reasonable person in it. Most stuck projects are full of people doing their best inside a structure that isn't working.
  • Tell your manager first and give them time to plan, so the team doesn't hear it secondhand.

Some guilt is normal. Good engineers feel responsible for unfinished work, especially when teammates are still in the middle of it. Responsibility has edges, though. You can care about a project without giving unlimited time to a structure that won't change. You can wish the team well and still stop paying a cost that no longer makes sense.

Leaving isn't a skill to use casually, and it isn't one to avoid forever either. Every month on a dead end is a month you aren't spending on something that can actually get better. If you're deciding right now, the question can be simple: is this hard because the work matters and the path is still getting clearer, or because the system refuses to learn? The first deserves patience. The second may deserve a careful goodbye.

Try this week

  • Score your project against the table above, and be honest about how long it's been in the right-hand column.
  • Write one kill criterion with a state and a date, and put it somewhere you'll see it.
  • Send one message asking for the specific decision you need, and name who can make it.
  • If you've decided to leave, start the handoff doc today, while the details are fresh.
